SJCS Team Incrementums ⅞pg. 1

Problem or Question
a) What does purple light do for plant growth in Moon regolith vs Earth soil?
Background
Purple light is highly beneficial for plant growth during the vegetative stage, as it
promotes the production of leaves and stems, which are crucial for flowering and
fruiting. Purple light, particularly when it leans toward the red spectrum, is ideal for
germinating seeds as it provides the necessary energy for chlorophyll production, a key
element in photosynthesis. This targeted spectrum ensures plants receive exactly what
they need to grow efficiently without expending energy on excess or wasted light ("How
the Lighting Color Spectrum Affects Plant Growth," 2024).
In the context of an experimental setup, we plan to sow seeds ¼-inch deep and space
them about 1 inch apart in rows that are 10 inches apart. To ensure optimal hydration,
the seeds will receive 5 milliliters of water daily on school days, totaling approximately
24.6 milliliters weekly. The arugula plants will be exposed to more than 6 hours of direct
sunlight per day, which aligns with their requirements for optimal growth ("How to Plant,
Grow, and Harvest Organic Arugula in a Raised Bed").
Additionally, purple light parallels the Moon's reflective properties. While the Moon does
not emit its own light, "moonlight" is sunlight reflected off its surface, with half the Moon
always in sunlight at any given time (Lunar Rocks, 2003). The lunar highlands, which
are located above the dark maria basins, experience extreme temperature variations,
ranging from approximately 390 K to 104 K, depending on the location and time of lunar
day (Lunar Rocks, 2003).
Hypothesis
If purple light is compared to natural light, then there will be more leaves, it will
flower faster, and overall it will grow better because it is documented that blue light
helps chlorophyll production, increases plant quality, maximizes growth, and quickly
helps with germination.
Blue light regulates stomata of plants and makes plants shorter, smaller, and
thicker, and with greener leaves. Plants grown under red light are usually tall with thin
leaves and lengthy height. Red light increases plant biomass and also creates faster
flowering times. Therefore, a combination of blue light and red light, in the form of purple
light will help the growth of the plant overall. Purple light should in theory cancel out the
negative effects of both the blue light and the red light alone. For example, a less
desirable trait of plants grown under blue light is that it makes plants in general shorter
and thicker. This trait should be canceled out by the red light's common trait of being
SJCS Team Incrementums ⅞pg. 2

taller and lengthy. We will test if the combined traits of red and blue light will help the
plants grow successfully in such harsh conditions as lunar soil, microgravity, and quick
changes in temperature, which are similar conditions that would be found on the moon.
Variables
b) Independent variable? Color of Light: purple
c) Dependent Variables ideas? Plant height and leaf color
d) Control? Natural Light, earth soil, arugula ( Roquette, heirloom non gmo
seeds) in all 4 set-ups

Procedure
1. Gather Materials
SJCS Team Incrementums ⅞pg. 3

2. Apply lab safety
a) lab goggles
b) disposable gloves
c) lab coat
d) hair tied up
3. Set up
a) assemble ( 50.8cm × 43.18cm × 33.02cm ) grow light containment box
b) assemble ( 15cm × 11cm × 11cm ) grow light stand
c) assemble purple grow light
d) fill 2 black planters (volume 343 cubic centimeters) with 311.15 cubic centimeters
of lunar highlands regolith
e) fill 2 black planters (volume 343 cubic centimeters) up to 5 cm mark
f)
place black planters in mini greenhouses
g) fit purple grow light into grow light containment box
Ex.:
h) turn on grow light
i)
place 1 lunar highlands regolith greenhouse and 1 earth soil greenhouse in grow
light containment box
j)
place 1 lunar highlands regolith greenhouse and 1 earth soil greenhouse in
windowsill
k) have 4 people do the following: plant 4 arugula seeds 0.635 cm deep and 2.54
cm apart in each greenhouse, close greenhouse lids.
l)
water each respective mini greenhouse with 5 ml of tap water each day
m) record data in data table
Regolith type
For the plant the moon challenge, the 7/8 class chose moon regolith, in place of
martian regolith. The reason for using moon regolith is because astronauts are going to
survey the moon before the planet Mars. Another intention for using moon regolith was
that our school was given a grant toward supplying the Lunar Regolith kits for this
experiment. In conclusion, we are grateful for the opportunity to work with moon
regolith.

Analysis/Graphs
SJCS Team Incrementums ⅞pg. 8

Conclusion
During our eight weeks in the PTMC, we faced a lot of challenges that helped us learn
how to adapt and solve problems. One big challenge was figuring out how much water
the plants needed to grow best. At first, we gave them 5 milliliters of water, but when
they didn’t grow much, we changed it to 20 milliliters, and they started growing better.
Our original hypothesis was that plants would grow better under purple light than natural
light. But the data in our chart rejects the hypothesis statement—plants under natural
light grew a lot better! This taught us how important it is to stay flexible and think
critically when things don’t go as planned in experiments.
Looking back, we saw ways to improve. For example, if we had started with more water
right away, the plants might have grown even better.
We also started asking new questions, like how astronauts can provide natural light for
plants in space, where sunlight doesn’t work the same way. Maybe advanced lighting or
reflective materials could help. It’s exciting to think about how science can solve these
problems.
The PTMC didn’t just teach us the steps of the scientific method; it made us curious
about space and agriculture. It showed us how experiments can connect to real-world
problems, and it inspired us to think about how we can be part of solving them.
